slides.title: Chapter 2: How Bitcoin Works
slides.say: Chapter 1 asked what Bitcoin is; this chapter follows one payment, Alice paying Bob's Store, from invoice to blockchain. Point at the wallet picture on the right, a real wallet of 2012. Ask who has used a wallet app. Every number in the deck was computed by the chapter's own library.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Six parts follow one payment from the invoice to the spending. Point at the ranges: each is a block of slides you can jump to. Ask the class which part they expect to be hardest. Three true stories and fourteen code examples are spread across the parts.
slides.takeaway: Six parts, three true stories, fourteen examples

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.say: These six questions are the chapter in miniature, and each has an answer on a slide. Read them aloud and ask students to guess the answer before the summary. A common mistake is to treat them as vocabulary; they are about how and why.

slides.title: The chapter in one picture
slides.say: Six steps carry one payment: invoice, transaction, coins, build, block, spend. Trace Alice's payment along the row with a finger. Ask where the money is at each step. Students often think coins move; only records of ownership change.
slides.takeaway: Six steps, one payment: from invoice to a spendable coin

slides.title: Buying from an Online Store
slides.say: Part 1 starts where Alice does, with an invoice from an online store. Point at the three cards: the whole system, the smallest unit and the link. Ask what the cent is to a dollar. Remind students that the cards are only a preview of the slides that follow.
slides.takeaway: Alice pays Bob's Store: one real payment, followed all the way

slides.title: Four roles, one network
slides.say: Four roles share the work: wallets sign, nodes check, miners bundle, and the blockchain is the shared record. Point at each box on the right and match it to the picture. Ask who owns the record; the answer is nobody. Do not call a wallet a purse of coins.
slides.takeaway: No single owner: wallets sign, nodes check, miners bundle

slides.title: Five free bitcoins for every visitor
slides.say: Alice needs bitcoin before she can pay, and in 2010 there was almost nowhere to buy it. Point at Andresen's photograph and at the link line. Ask why anyone would give coins away. Say that this is a true story with a source the students can open.
slides.takeaway: Before exchanges, distribution itself had to be invented

slides.title: Satoshis are whole numbers
slides.say: Bitcoin counts in satoshis, one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin. Point at the result card: whole numbers in, the same text back. Ask why decimals are risky for money. The common mistake is to compute with floating point, which loses digits.
slides.takeaway: Inside the network every amount is a whole number of satoshis

slides.title: Reading Bob's invoice
slides.say: BIP 21 defines the link that wallets and QR codes use. Point at the code lines, then at the result card, now full width. Ask which three facts the wallet reads from the link. Remember that the query text is URL-encoded, so the apostrophe appears as %27.
slides.takeaway: One link carries the address, the amount and the label

slides.title: What is inside Bob's payment link
slides.say: Bob's link is one string with five parts. Point at the colour of each segment and read it aloud. Ask what the wallet does when it meets the word bitcoin followed by a colon. A common mistake is to think the QR code is encrypted; it only holds this text.
slides.takeaway: One string carries the address, the amount and the label

slides.title: Bitcoin Transactions
slides.say: Part 2 opens the payment itself. A transaction spends earlier outputs and creates new ones, and the difference is the fee. Point at the banknote analogy on the first card. Ask what happens to the part of a banknote you do not need.
slides.takeaway: Inputs, outputs, chains and change

slides.title: Inputs and outputs
slides.say: A transaction is double-entry bookkeeping: inputs on the left, outputs on the right, and the difference is the fee. Point at the arrows of figure 2-2. Ask which side holds the coins. A common mistake is to think an input contains money; it only points.
slides.takeaway: An input spends an earlier output; an output creates a new one

slides.title: Alice's transaction is a balanced ledger line
slides.say: The picture is the ledger line of Alice's payment. Point at the two bars: they have the same length, so inputs equal outputs plus fee. Ask which part the miner collects. A common mistake is to look for the fee as a field; it is only what is left over.
slides.takeaway: Every satoshi that goes in is either claimed by an output or left to the miner

slides.title: Inputs equal outputs plus the fee
slides.say: Inputs add up to 100,000 satoshis and outputs to 95,000, so 5,000 is implied and collected by the miner. Point at the chart: the three slices equal the input. Ask where the fee is written; the answer is nowhere. Students often hunt for a fee field that does not exist.
slides.takeaway: Whatever the outputs do not claim becomes the miner's fee

slides.title: The txid is shown backwards
slides.say: Inside a transaction the earlier identifier is stored in one byte order, and explorers print the reverse. Point at the first eight hex digits in the table, which differ. Ask why two tools disagree about the same value. A common mistake is to paste the stored form into an explorer.
slides.takeaway: Explorers show the identifier in reverse byte order

slides.title: How one output is named and found
slides.say: Here three names meet. Point at the outpoint on the right: a transaction identifier, a colon and an output number. Ask which outputs are still coins. Remind students that the bytes are stored in the opposite order to the one explorers display.
slides.takeaway: An input never holds coins; it names an earlier output by its identifier and number

slides.title: Size in virtual bytes and the fee rate
slides.say: The transaction weighs 569 units, which is 143 virtual bytes, and the 5,000 satoshi fee gives about 35 satoshis per byte. Point at the rounding up. Ask why miners care about the rate rather than the fee. Students often divide by the weight instead of the virtual size.
slides.takeaway: Miners rank transactions by fee per virtual byte

slides.title: Size, weight and the fee rate
slides.say: Follow the numbers down the left: 125 plain bytes count four each, 69 witness bytes count once, giving 569 weight units. Ask why signatures are discounted. A common mistake is to divide the fee by bytes instead of virtual bytes.
slides.takeaway: Signature bytes are discounted, and miners rank by fee per virtual byte

slides.title: A chain of transactions
slides.say: Figure 2-3 shows three linked transactions. Point at one arrow and read the output it names. Ask how to find where a coin began. A spent output can never be spent again, which is the whole defence against double spending.
slides.takeaway: Follow the arrows backwards to find where a coin came from

slides.title: Which outputs are still unspent
slides.say: Collecting what was spent leaves the unspent outputs, and those are the coins that exist. Point at the three outputs in the result. Ask what a wallet balance is; the answer is the sum of unspent outputs it can sign for. Spent and unspent are not the same as old and new.
slides.takeaway: Unspent outputs are the coins that exist right now

slides.title: A lock, a key and a string of bytes
slides.say: Point at the lock on the output and the key on the input, then at the byte fields below. Ask what a script can demand besides a signature. Students often think Bitcoin scripts are a general programming language; they are small on purpose.
slides.takeaway: A script locks the output, and serialization turns the whole transaction into bytes

slides.title: Coin Selection
slides.say: Part 3 asks how a wallet chooses what to spend. Coins are spent whole, so the choice decides the change. Point at the three cards. Ask what you do when you only have a large banknote.
slides.takeaway: Which coins to spend, and what shape the payment takes

slides.title: Coin selection: pick, pay, change back
slides.say: A wallet cannot cut a coin in half, so it takes whole coins until the payment is covered and sends the surplus back as change. Point at the chart: the picked coins and the change bar. Ask what would happen without change. Real wallets use smarter rules than this one.
slides.takeaway: Coins are taken whole, so the surplus returns as change

slides.title: Chains, change and the choice of coins
slides.say: Read the chain left to right: grey outputs are spent, teal ones are coins. Point at the 20,000 output, which is Alice's change. Ask why coin selection matters for privacy and fees. Change is an ordinary output to a new address of the payer.
slides.takeaway: Spent outputs make the chain; unspent outputs are the coins

slides.title: Three common shapes of a transaction
slides.say: Payment, consolidation and batching are three shapes of the same ledger rule: inputs minus outputs is the fee. Point at the table rows. Ask which shape a business paying salaries would use. Do not confuse consolidation with mixing coins.
slides.takeaway: The same ledger rule fits every shape

slides.title: Three common shapes, counted in satoshis
slides.say: The same rule appears three times: inputs minus outputs is the fee. Point at the fees under each shape. Ask which shape saves the most per payee. Consolidation is best done when fees are low.
slides.takeaway: The same ledger rule holds whether one coin or many are spent

slides.title: Constructing a Transaction
slides.say: Part 4 builds Alice's transaction: find inputs, write outputs, leave a fee, sign. Point at the cheque analogy on the middle card. Ask who decides the fee; the wallet does. The fee rate decides how much change comes back.
slides.takeaway: The wallet assembles, prices and signs the payment

slides.title: From coins to a signed transaction
slides.say: The wallet builds the transaction in five steps and only decides inputs, outputs and fee; the rules do the rest. Point at the sums under step 3. Ask which step needs the private key; it is step 4. Students often think the wallet sends coins, when it sends a signed record.
slides.takeaway: The wallet only decides inputs, outputs and fee; the rules do the rest

slides.title: From a dollar price to a signed payment
slides.say: Follow the six boxes from the dollar price to the output. Ask why the invoice must be paid soon. Point at the whole-number step: the wallet never works with decimals. Do not call the wallet a purse that holds coins; it holds keys.
slides.takeaway: The wallet turns the shop's price and address into an output you can sign

slides.title: A higher fee rate leaves less change
slides.say: A higher fee rate leaves less change, because the fee is rate times size. Point at the falling bars. Ask what rate Alice should pick when she is in no hurry. A common mistake is to treat the fee as a percentage of the payment; it depends on size.
slides.takeaway: The wallet decides the fee; the change is what remains

slides.title: Fingerprints and key pairs
slides.say: The two hashes differ completely though the texts differ by one digit. Point at the one-way arrows on the right. Ask which direction is easy. A common mistake is to say the public key can be turned back into the private one; that is infeasible.
slides.takeaway: A hash fingerprints data; a key pair separates checking from signing

slides.title: Signatures, checks and secrecy
slides.say: Walk through signing on the top row and checking on the bottom. Point at the changed character that breaks the checksum. Ask whether anything is hidden in a transaction. Students confuse signing with encrypting; here nothing is hidden.
slides.takeaway: A signature proves approval; a checksum catches slips; nothing is hidden

slides.title: Adding the Transaction to the Blockchain
slides.say: Part 5 follows the signed transaction into a block. Point at the dice analogy for mining and the witness analogy for confirmations. Ask why page one of a ledger matters. Each block on top makes reversal harder.
slides.takeaway: From a node's inbox to a block that others build on

slides.title: Who takes part in the network
slides.say: Point at the full nodes in the middle and the lightweight clients at the edge. Ask what a lightweight client has to trust. There is no server here; every line is a link between equals, and all participants are peers.
slides.takeaway: Every participant is a peer; they differ in how much they check for themselves

slides.title: How a payment spreads
slides.say: Trace the spread ring by ring: one wallet, a few nodes, then many. Point at the check each node makes before forwarding. Ask why the route does not matter. Gossip needs no coordinator, so the spread is fast and hard to stop.
slides.takeaway: Each node checks a payment and passes it on, so it reaches the miners

slides.title: The waiting room and the window
slides.say: Point at the pool sorted by fee rate and at the bracket that marks the next block. Ask where Bob sees the payment first. An explorer is only a window; the pool of one node can differ from another's.
slides.takeaway: Transactions wait in the pool; an explorer lets anyone watch them reach a block

slides.title: What a miner builds
slides.say: Show a block as a header of six fields plus a list of transactions, the coinbase first. Point at the 80-byte total. Ask what the miner hashes; it is the header only. A candidate block becomes a block only with a proof of work.
slides.takeaway: A block is a header of 80 bytes plus a list of transactions

slides.title: Height, depth and confirmations
slides.say: Alice's transaction sits in block 277,316. Height counts up from the genesis block and depth counts the blocks on top. Point at figure 2-7 and ask how many confirmations Alice has after three more blocks. Height and depth are different numbers.
slides.takeaway: More blocks on top means a payment that is harder to reverse

slides.title: Confirmations counted on a ruler
slides.say: The ruler runs from the genesis block to Alice's block and beyond. Point at the dashed box: before a block, the payment is unconfirmed. Ask how many confirmations after block 277,318. Height and confirmations are different counts.
slides.takeaway: Each block on top of Alice's makes her payment harder to reverse

slides.title: One more zero, many more tries
slides.say: A miner changes the nonce and hashes again until the result starts with enough zeros. Point at the log-scale bars: each extra zero costs about sixteen times more tries. Ask how anyone can check the answer fast. The result is luck, not skill, and no shortcut exists.
slides.takeaway: Mining is a search; more zeros means more work

slides.title: Bytes, hex, entropy and nonce
slides.say: Use the byte 0xEB to move between bits, hex and decimal. Point at the nonce table: one number changes the whole hash, and 33 is the first that starts with a zero. Ask how many digits 256 bits need in decimal. Do not mix up bits and bytes.
slides.takeaway: A nonce changes the hash; entropy and bytes size the search

slides.title: The first block header is 80 bytes
slides.say: The genesis block was mined on 3 January 2009; its header packs six fields into 80 bytes. Point at the nonce row. Ask why the name starts with ten zeros. Hashing twice and reversing the bytes is the step students forget.
slides.takeaway: A block's name is the hash of its 80-byte header

slides.title: Trees, targets and the pace of mining
slides.say: Build the tree from the bottom: pairs of hashes up to one root. Point at the target line on the right and the hash below it. Ask what changes when the difficulty rises. Difficulty moves every 2,016 blocks, not every block.
slides.takeaway: One root commits to all transactions, and one target sets the pace

slides.title: When two blocks compete
slides.say: Two blocks arrive at the same height, and the next block decides. Point at the longer branch. Ask what happens to the transactions in the loser. A double spend fails because only one of two conflicting transactions can be in the best chain.
slides.takeaway: The chain with the most work wins, and the loser's transactions return to the pool

slides.title: Nine pages, one table of probabilities
slides.say: The white paper reached readers on 31 October 2008, and its section 11 computes the attacker's odds. Point at the bust and at the source link. Ask what question a mathematician would ask about confirmations. Say that Satoshi Nakamoto is a pseudonym.
slides.takeaway: A confirmation is a probability statement, and you can compute it

slides.title: Nakamoto's catch-up table, recomputed
slides.say: Rerunning the formula gives the paper's table to seven places. Point at the two lines: the attacker with 10 percent and with 30 percent of the power. Ask why six confirmations became a habit. A larger attacker never makes the odds vanish, only smaller.
slides.takeaway: Every confirmation makes a reversal much less likely

slides.title: How many confirmations are enough
slides.say: Read the table downwards: each confirmation shrinks the attacker's chance. Point at the two columns. Ask what a shop selling a coffee should require. The number of confirmations is an economic choice, not a technical rule.
slides.takeaway: The more it costs to lose, the more confirmations a seller waits for

slides.title: Spending the Transaction
slides.say: Part 6 closes the loop: Bob spends his output, and every node checks the same rules. Point at the chess analogy. Ask what happens to a block that breaks a rule. It is refused by everyone, and its miner earns nothing.
slides.takeaway: When Bob may spend, and what every node checks first

slides.title: The reward halves every 210,000 blocks
slides.say: The reward is a consensus rule: every node computes it the same way and refuses a block that claims more. Point at the halving steps and the full-width result. Ask why the total is capped. Halving is a rule, not a promise of price.
slides.takeaway: Halving is a rule every node enforces, not a promise

slides.title: Where new coins come from
slides.say: Point at the coinbase: no input, one output to the miner. Next to it, show the sudoku, hard to fill and quick to check. Ask who pays for mining. The pool diagram shows many small miners sharing one reward in proportion to their shares.
slides.takeaway: The first transaction of each block creates the coins that pay for mining

slides.title: The day someone printed 184 billion bitcoin
slides.say: On 15 August 2010 block 74,638 created about 184 billion bitcoin out of an overflow. Point at the date and at the source link. Ask which rule was missing. Say that the network fixed itself in hours because every node checks every rule.
slides.takeaway: Validation by every node is the immune system - and it worked

slides.title: Two outputs that wrapped around
slides.say: Two huge outputs summed to a negative number in 64 bits, so the old check passed. Point at the table row 'Stored in 64 bits'. Ask what a range check would have done. The common mistake is to think the attacker broke cryptography; no key was broken.
slides.takeaway: One overflow created 184 billion bitcoin; one new rule ended it

slides.title: The rules and how they change
slides.say: Rules are checks every full node makes. Point at the nested boxes: a soft fork shrinks the valid set, a hard fork enlarges it. Ask which one old nodes survive. A hard fork is not just a big upgrade; it splits nodes that stay behind.
slides.takeaway: A rule change is safe when old nodes still accept the new blocks

slides.title: Spending onward, and checking with a short proof
slides.say: Spending onward extends the chain: Bob's output becomes the input to his payment. Point at the merkle path of three hashes. Ask how a phone checks a block of thousands without downloading it. The proof shows inclusion, not that the payment is wise.
slides.takeaway: Bob's wallet can prove a payment with a handful of hashes

slides.title: The chain written as a graph of statements
slides.say: The chain can be written as triples: subject, predicate, object. Point at the three kinds of node: entity, activity and agent. Ask what question a graph can answer that a list cannot. An ontology is a model of the field, not a database.
slides.takeaway: Outputs, transactions and key holders are things, activities and agents

slides.title: Five pages to try the mechanism yourself
slides.say: Each demonstration page adds one idea: hash, block, chain, peers, coinbase. Point at the ladder and ask students to predict what breaks when an early block is edited. Say that trying each page for five minutes teaches more than rereading the slide.
slides.takeaway: Each page adds one idea to the one before it

slides.title: Summary: the six answers
slides.say: Each row answers one of the six opening questions in a line. Ask students to cover the right column and answer from memory. Point back to slide 3. A student who can use the everyday pictures to explain each answer has the chapter.
slides.takeaway: Inputs, outputs, fee, mining, confirmations, rules

slides.title: Resources: read, try, watch, ask
slides.say: These links are open and free. Start with the chapter source and the white paper, then paste a real transaction into the block explorer. Ask which resource each student will try this week. Treat the explorer as a reading tool, never as a place to enter keys.

slides.title: Questions?
